newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: FEATURE-Filipina cadets evoke old combat questions.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Filipina cadets evoke old combat questions.

text.p: Seven women who became the first female military academy graduates in the Philippines have stirred a debate in a country where the woman's only place, Ferdinand Marcos once said, is in the bedroom.

Four years after admitting its first non-male candidates, the 92-year-old Philippine Military Academy (PMA) last month graduated the seven female cadets who believe they have as much right as men to fight on the front-lines.
That was unthinkable scarcely more than a decade ago.
"The only place for a woman is in the bedroom," Marcos said derisively in 1985 after Corazon Aquino challenged the long-entrenched strongman in a snap presidential election.
Months later, confronted by a "people power" revolt Aquino had inspired, Marcos fled his palace to die in exile in Hawaii.
BASTION OF MACHISMO
A bastion of machismo that has produced some of the country's best fighting men, the academy sprawled on a mountain resort in northern Baguio city has also had to swallow its pride.
Now, a woman mannequin stands alongside a line-up of five male models in its hall, symbolising the transformation of the PMA's grey and white cadet uniforms from 1908 to the present.
Four of the PMA's first seven women graduates will join the Army, two the Air Force and one the Navy.
But all still face an old question: will they be allowed to fight on the front-lines?
No, says former armed forces chief of staff Rodolfo Biazon.

"I am not being sexist," he said. "But you know we have to contend with the biological nature and the difference of the two sexes. Men are more muscle-bound and they can do some things better than women can."
COMBAT DEBATE REVIVED
That has spurred editorials and articles in the press, leading one magazine to even explore how the seven coped with their menstrual cycles while in training.
Biazon contends women should not be put in the Army or Marines, but could serve in the Navy or Air Force, where their duties would not rely on mere physical strength.
Army chief Lieutenant General Clemente Mariano takes the opposite tack, saying there will be "equal opportunities" for women officers with "minimal restrictions" due to their physique.
"Opportunities will greatly depend on their capabilities," he said recently.
WOMEN CADETS SEE OPPORTUNITIES
The group of seven, winnowed down from 16 PMA female aspirants, say they are optimistic about being given a chance.

Even if not used on the front-lines, "we will be allowed to join other combat support units like field artillery," said Army-bound Leah Lorenzo, who ranked third in her 123-member graduating class and was the top-ranked woman graduate of PMA.
But the chance to fight alongside men is important, said Victoria Blancaflor, 23, who is also joining the Army.
"If we won't be given those combat assignments, we won't be promoted as progressively as our male counterparts," she said.
WOMEN ALREADY IN RANKS
Women have been part of the Philippines military before this year's barrier-breaking graduates, with more than 1,600 in the armed forces out of about 117,000 of its total personnel.
But they were usually recruited for the Women's Auxiliary Corp, where they worked in communications and at desk jobs.
The Army has produced two female generals, both from the nursing corp.
WOMEN IN MILITARY A QUESTION ELSEWHERE
The debate over women in the military is reverberating in other countries, including the United States.
Last month, a committee at the U.S. Citadel military academy faulted its officials for their treatment of women and recommended that the formerly all-male academy hire more female officers.
Two women who enrolled at the Citadel last autumn dropped out this year, charging they had been harassed.

Even though the Philippines has had a women president in its recent history with Aquino, the gates of the PMA had to be cracked open by a new law that mandates women as equal partners in the country's development.
But integration was not easy.
"It took some time...constant dialogue, constant talks with the male cadets," PMA Superintendent Victor Mayo told Reuters.
"A lot of the portion of credit goes to the female cadets," he said. "They proved they can do it."
LEGACY CONTINUES
After the breakthrough batch of women, the PMA currently has 42 women out of its 840 student body and expects an additional 18 or 19 females to join this month for its graduating class of 2001.

Asked about the lessons learned from the pioneering batch, a first-year female cadet said: "Once you know what you want in life, and are willing to work hard for as long as it takes, there isn't anything you can't do."
